name: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
title: Who Uses AI in the Early Grades
answer: In preschool through second grade, general AI tools are mostly not designed for young children, so student use is limited and adult controlled. The largest benefit and smallest risk come from teacher use, such as preparing stories, picture schedules, family notes, and summaries of observations. Schools should be able to name the adult who set up any AI tool and the adult who is watching when a young child uses it.

sections.body: The idea is that the early grades are a different case for AI. Most general tools assume adult or older student users, and some offer no student accounts at all or require a school setup or parental consent for children under 13. UNESCO guidance puts 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI, which is far beyond preschool and the early primary years. The problem this solves is confusion about whether young children should use AI directly. The chapter's answer is to focus on teacher use, where the benefits are largest and the risks smallest, while keeping any child use under clear adult responsibility.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool through second grade, the text describes teacher use as the main practice. An early childhood teacher can use AI to write short stories at a child's level, make picture schedules, draft family notes, and turn scattered observations into clear summaries. Saving time on those tasks gives the teacher more minutes on the floor with children. For student use, the text notes that tools differ: ChatGPT for Teachers is designed for educators only and offers no student accounts, MagicSchool requires educator accounts to belong to adults and students use it only through a school's own setup, and Canva for Education lets teachers invite students but requires parental consent for students under 13. The text does not give separate practices for preschool, kindergarten, first grade, and second grade beyond saying a preschooler or first grader is years away from independent AI conversations.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not present a study or an evidence label for this idea. It points to broader guidance, stating that UNESCO recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI (Miao & Holmes, 2023). It also describes the design rules of several tools, such as educator accounts for adults and parental consent for students under 13. On that basis, the chapter's claim about teacher use rests on practice and guidance rather than research evidence. The text gives no measured finding about learning gains from AI in the early grades.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits start with age and supervision. The text says a preschooler or first grader is years away from the age of 13 that UNESCO recommends for independent conversations with generative AI. When a young child uses an AI tool, the school should be able to name the adult who set it up and the adult who is watching. Tools also set their own conditions: some are for educators only, some require a school setup, and some require parental consent for students under 13. The decisions that stay with people include whether to use a tool with children at all, who sets it up, who supervises, and how to handle consent, while the teacher remains responsible for the classroom tasks and the time saved is meant to return to children.
